excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content:
That log is because the PoW chain re-orged deeper than the ETH1_FOLLOW_DISTANCE. That’s because Kiln had a really unstable PoW network (one GPU miner was a superpower) and a very short follow distance (16 blocks rather than 2048 on mainnet). Re-orgs of such a depth aren’t supported by the protocol, we need social consensus to resolve them. 

It’s not a bug IMO, it’s an artifact of the test environment (Kiln). It would be great if we could test on something exactly like mainnet, but unfortunately that’s much easier said than done.

excerpts.author: mariusvanderwijden
excerpts.content: We can test that via shadow forking on mainnet

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content:
I do wonder if we should be using the mainnet follow distance for these testnets.

Although I don’t think it would make make a difference for Lighthouse, if we’re going to be merging with the “Eth1” chain then it does seem like we should be using eth1 params as close as possible to mainnet.

I assume the follow distance was dropped in prior testnets for UX reasons (e.g., faster deposits). I wonder if these benefits are really worth the deviance from mainnet specs.

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content:
It’s been a while, but I believe LH will self heal if the fork is resolved (ie we switch back to the original fork) or once the cache gets sufficient old. I’m not certain about the latter, but I’ll check.

Either way the —purge-eth1-cache flag will always solve it manually.

If validators manage to vote in a conflicting Eth1 data to the beacon state there will be liveness failure at the protocol level.

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content: Yeah, I am wondering about the latter. In the post-Merge world  this should not happen as if jump from one fork to another happens the voting result from the previous fork will be reverted, and the new one will take precedence

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content:
It seems likely that what you described will happen, but it’s not guaranteed. There are no checks in state transition to ensure eth1_data is consistent with exec payloads.

Presently LH “eth1 voting” is a separate system to the new execution payload functionally. There’s nothing ensuring they have a 1:1 mapping, although it’s very likely they will be 1:1 in practice. 

I will think about what it would take to ensure that 1:1 mapping.

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content: I think the current Eth1 voting scheme looks pretty ugly in a post-merge world.

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content: We have two sources of truth for the execution chain. I’m sure this isn’t news to anyone, though.

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content: My gut is that it's gonna be 1:1 post-Merge as you vote for a canonical chain and you build blocks including Eth1Data on the canonical chain as well. So, likely 1:1, tho edge cases are possible

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content: Yeah, you actually set the head, and then query if the head has been changed to incorporate the head into proposer voting in a separate process

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content:
Clients may want to ensure that the same RPC is used for payloads and Eth1 voting.

If users happen to make a mistake and use Infura for Eth1 and local EE for payloads then we have a risk of two conflicting sources of truth. Very small risk IMO, but something to consider.

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content: I think that CL clients should use an EE url provided by the user for communicating with EL and supporting a legacy poll process to avoid such a conflict

excerpts.author: jlokier
excerpts.content:
>  do wonder if we should be using the mainnet follow distance for these testnets.

I think the low follow distance has made this Kiln merge more of a valuable test.  It's one of the advantages of using weaker parameters in test environments.  In this case it looks like one GPU miner caused unexpected harm, but seeing unexpected things happen is a benefit of the testnet being public.

On Mainnet it seems not entirely outrageous to imagine a mining/staking consortium deciding to throw every rig they have (with the ASICs about to become redundant) at destabilising the PoS merge. Even if there was only a bump that was self-healing, it might provide a financial advantage to the organised during the bump and recovery phase.
